caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No — and the man who made it wanted that proved.

In 1868 a New York tobacconist named George Hull lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4 and the giants it says once lived on Earth. Angered by the credulity around him, he set out to show how easily people could be fooled.

He had a block of gypsum 10 feet 4½ inches long quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling the workmen it was for a Lincoln monument. In Chicago two sculptors carved it in Hull's own likeness, hairless — a geologist had told him hair would not petrify. Sand and water, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles in a board aged the surface. Cost: $2,600.

The figure was buried on his cousin William Newell's farm in late November 1868 and "found" on October 16, 1869, by two men hired to dig a well. Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute look. Three to five hundred people came a day.

Andrew D. White, Cornell's first president, pointed out there was no reason to dig a well in that spot. Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh saw fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum and called it "a most decided humbug". Hull confessed on December 10, 1869. On February 2, 1870, his giant and P. T. Barnum's plaster copy were both ruled fakes in court.

Still open: whether Edward Burkhardt, the Chicago stonecutter, knew what he was making. And the Michigan arcade displaying a copy says theirs is Barnum's.

Images: a 1910 Bain News Service negative of the giant, the "Onondaga Giant" lithograph from Popular Graphic Arts, and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Iowa, scanned by NYPL.

cards.headline: Nobody needed a well. <y>They found a giant.</y>
cards.alt: Pale stone figure of a man lying in a shallow pit of dark earth beside a root.

cards.headline: Ten feet four and a half inches, <y>carved to look like Hull</y>
cards.note: A print sold as "The Onondaga Giant" showed the right and left sides, as he appears lying in state. George Hull, a New York tobacconist, had the figure made in his own form.
cards.source: The Onondaga Giant, Popular Graphic Arts · public domain
cards.alt: Lithograph of a reclining nude stone figure on a plinth, drawn in grey chalk.

cards.headline: The stone came from <y>a gypsum quarry in Iowa</y>
cards.note: In 1868 Hull hired men to quarry a block of gypsum at Fort Dodge, Iowa. He told them it was for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York.
cards.source: View in Cardiff Glen, Iowa, 1873 · NYPL scan
cards.alt: Wooded rock face above a slope of broken pale stone blocks, sepia photograph.

cards.headline: A souvenir card printed <y>the names of the hoaxers</y>
cards.note: The reverse of the stereocard states the block was taken to Chicago, the giant carved, then shipped to New York and buried in a barn lot. It names the perpetrators of the imposture as George Hull and H. B. Martin.
cards.source: Stereocard reverse, Cardiff Glen, 1873 · NYPL scan
cards.alt: Printed text on pink card headed VIEW IN CARDIFF GLEN, with pencil and ink notes.

cards.headline: No hair, and <y>tool marks still fresh</y>
cards.note: Hull removed the hair and beard after a geologist told him hair does not petrify. Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh noted that soluble gypsum buried for centuries in wet earth would not keep fresh tool marks. He called it "a most decided humbug".
cards.alt: Close view of the smooth, bald stone head and shoulders of the buried figure.

cards.headline: Both giants were <y>ruled fakes in court</y>
cards.note: Hull confessed on December 10, 1869; on February 2, 1870, his giant and Barnum's copy were declared fakes. It is still not clear whether the Chicago stonecutter who took the block knew what it was for.
cards.source: View in Cardiff Glen, Iowa, 1873 · NYPL scan
cards.alt: Sunlit ledge of pale quarry rock among trees, faded sepia stereograph half.
